title: An Isolated Act of Dishonesty Doesn't Have to End Your Career — And Now There's a Published Case to Prove It
excerpt: A published California appellate decision limits when a single act of dishonesty can justify firing a peace officer. Departments have long treated any dishonesty finding as an automatic termination, but the court says a more searching, individualized analysis is required — with real consequences for POST decertification cases.

title: The City Tried to Skip the Bargaining Table on Your Pension. The Court Sent Back the Bill.
excerpt: A California appellate ruling confirms that when a city unilaterally changes pension reciprocity, it still owes employees a seat at the table — and a check to make up the difference. The case traces back to a 2010 decision by one city to sever reciprocity between its main pension system and a smaller retirement plan without ever bargaining the fallout.

title: Banked Your Vacation Hours for Retirement? The California Supreme Court Just Redrew the Math.
excerpt: The California Supreme Court limits how much banked leave can count toward your final pension calculation under PEPRA — even if your final compensation period spans two calendar years. The ruling closes a workaround some legacy county retirement system members used to stack two annual cashout caps into one inflated payout.

title: Monday-Morning Quarterbacking a Life-or-Death Decision: Why One Appeals Court Finally Said Enough
excerpt: A Texas appellate reversal reinforces the reasonable-officer standard that also governs California's deadly force law, rejecting hindsight-driven second-guessing of split-second decisions. The court's reasoning is a useful citation anytime a prosecutor or plaintiff's attorney tries to dissect an officer's split-second call with the benefit of months of calm reflection.

title: The Supreme Court Just Staked Hawaii's "Vampire Rule" Through the Heart — California Should Take Notice
excerpt: The U.S. Supreme Court strikes down Hawaii's default ban on concealed carry at private property open to the public, closing off a workaround California had been eyeing for its own restrictions. Hawaii's so-called “vampire rule” flipped ordinary property law on its head, and the Court wasn't willing to let that stand.

title: A Bill Meant to Rein In Federal Agents Could Leave California Officers Holding the Bag
excerpt: Senate Bill 747 aims to hold federal agents accountable, but its current language could create a second, murkier standard of qualified immunity for California's own peace officers. The bill was written to target federal overreach, yet the way it's drafted could sweep in officers who had nothing to do with the conduct it was meant to address.

title: Those Minutes Before Roll Call? The Feds Just Said They Count
excerpt: A new federal opinion letter confirms that essential pre- and post-shift tasks like gear checks and equipment prep are compensable work, not free time. Every shift has a shadow shift attached to it, and departments that have treated those minutes as unpaid now have a federal opinion working against that practice.

title: A Federal Court Just Narrowed a Wage Claim — Here's Why California First Responders Don't Need to Panic
excerpt: A Third Circuit ruling narrows federal 'gap time' wage claims in that circuit, but Ninth Circuit precedent and California wage law keep the door open for California police and fire employees. Gap time — straight-time hours worked below the 40-hour threshold during an overtime week — has long been a gray area in wage litigation.

title: Before Your Personnel File Goes Public, Shouldn't Someone Have to Tell You?
excerpt: A New York labor board ruling says agencies must bargain over advance notice before releasing personnel records — persuasive authority for California officers under Penal Code 832.7. After New York repealed the law shielding disciplinary records, unions demanded a voice in exactly how and when those records get released.

title: Trying to Switch Unions Through the Back Door? PERB Just Nailed That Door Shut
excerpt: Two PERB decisions confirm that severance petitions can only be used to create a brand-new standalone bargaining unit — not to transfer classifications into an existing one. The shortcut some unions have tried — carving a specialized group out of one unit and redirecting them straight into another — doesn't fly under this reading of the statute.

title: Disciplined AND Retaliated Against? Why Losing One Fight Doesn't Mean You Lose the War
excerpt: An appellate ruling confirms that an arbitrator can order back pay for union retaliation even after a state personnel board has already upheld the same discipline on other grounds. A personnel board sign-off on the merits of a suspension doesn't automatically close the door on a separate retaliation claim over the same conduct.

title: Your K9's Bite File Just Got a Lot More Public — Here's the Case That Did It
excerpt: A published appellate ruling redefines 'great bodily injury' for purposes of personnel-record disclosure, and canine bite reports are now squarely in the blast radius. Agencies that have quietly classified K9 bites as minor to keep files confidential now have a published decision working against that practice.

title: The County Thought a Contract Clause Let It Skip the Bargaining Table. The Court of Appeal Disagreed.
excerpt: A published ruling holds that vague 'reorganization' language in an MOU isn't enough to waive a union's right to bargain over outsourcing — agencies need something a lot more explicit. The County tried to lean on boilerplate management-rights language to skip the bargaining table entirely, and the Court of Appeal wasn't buying it.

title: How Your Overtime Rate Gets Calculated Just Became a Ninth Circuit Fight — And Firefighters Have Skin in the Game
excerpt: A district court got the math right on how salaried firefighters' regular rate of pay should be calculated under the FLSA. Now the City is appealing, and the stakes are statewide — more than 32,000 career firefighters have overtime checks riding on how the divisor question gets resolved.

title: A Federal Court Just Blew a Hole in California's Mask-Ban Law — But Don't Celebrate Yet If You're Not Federal
excerpt: The Ninth Circuit sided with the federal government on the No Vigilantes Act's ID mandate, citing the Supremacy Clause — a ruling that leaves state and local officers holding the restrictions federal agents just escaped. The companion facial-covering law remains fully in force against California's own peace officers.

title: Off the Clock Doesn't Mean Off the Radar — But It Also Doesn't Mean Off Your Rights
excerpt: A federal court sides with an officer disciplined for off-duty protest activity, reinforcing that public employers can't punish speech on matters of public concern just because a badge is involved. The ruling applies the familiar Pickering balancing test and comes down hard in the officer's favor.

title: The 'Clean Slate' Deal Is Dead — What AB 1388 Actually Changes for Discipline Cases
excerpt: As of January 1, 2026, agencies and officers can no longer strike 'clean record agreements' to quietly settle discipline disputes. Here's what that means for pending and future cases — expect fewer negotiated resolutions and more disputes pushed all the way through the full appeal process.

title: The Jury Cleared LAPD in the Burlington Shooting. The Fight Isn't Over.
excerpt: A Burbank jury delivered a 9-3 defense verdict for the City in one of California's most closely watched officer-involved shooting cases. Now the plaintiffs want a do-over, arguing the court wrongly excluded internal command testimony that could have changed the outcome — and a hearing is set to decide it.

title: Industrial Disability Retirement Isn't the Same as Regular Retirement — Here's Why That Distinction Pays
excerpt: Getting classified as an industrial (rather than ordinary) disability retirement can mean the difference between a fraction of your pension and a tax-advantaged benefit that reflects what the job actually cost you. Retirement systems don't volunteer the stronger classification — the application has to affirmatively earn it.

title: Fired, Then Vindicated: A Record Verdict for a Wrongfully Terminated Police Lieutenant Survives Appeal
excerpt: The Court of Appeal affirmed a record jury verdict in favor of a UC Santa Cruz police lieutenant who was wrongfully fired — a reminder that a bad termination decision doesn't just cost a career, it costs the agency. The university's bid to reduce or reverse the verdict on appeal came up empty.

title: A Fire Engine's Door Swung Open at an Emergency Scene — Now There's a Lawsuit. Here's Why It Might Not Go Far.
excerpt: A California driver is suing a fire department after an engine's door struck his truck at an emergency scene, but the suit may be running straight into a statute most plaintiffs' attorneys forget to check. California law provides real, specific protections for apparatus operating at an active emergency scene.

title: SDPD Has Been Quietly Filing Away 4 Out of Every 5 Complaints as 'Miscellaneous.' A Lawsuit Says That's Illegal.
excerpt: A new writ of mandate argues San Diego PD is using a label that doesn't exist anywhere in the governing law to keep the vast majority of misconduct complaints away from independent civilian review. Roughly 80 percent of all complaints have reportedly been filed under a 'miscellaneous' category the ordinance never authorized.

title: Eleven Years, Three Lawsuits, One $3.1 Million Answer to 'Why Didn't You Just Let It Go?'
excerpt: A veteran San Diego sergeant who reported racist material in department trainings spent over a decade fighting retaliation claims. The city just agreed the fight was worth $3.1 million — a reminder that unresolved complaints about training materials can metastasize into years of costly litigation.

title: Hurt on the Job by Someone Else's Negligence? The Rules on Who Gets Paid First Just Changed
excerpt: SB 487 rewrites how workers' compensation subrogation works for peace officers and firefighters hurt by a third party, guaranteeing a bigger cut of limited insurance proceeds actually reaches the injured employee. The law also closes a loophole that let employers treat a third-party settlement as a credit against future comp benefits.

title: The Heart Presumption Just Got Bigger — Here's Who's Newly Covered
excerpt: AB 1125 extends California's heart-injury workers' comp presumption to peace officers at the Department of State Hospitals who were previously left out of protections their counterparts already had. The presumption shifts the burden onto the employer to rebut a work-related cause, rather than making the officer prove it from scratch.

title: Airport Firefighters Just Caught Up to Everyone Else on Cancer and PTSD Coverage
excerpt: SB 230 closes a gap that left commercial airport firefighters without the same cancer and psychiatric injury presumptions their municipal and county counterparts have had for years. The expanded coverage also reaches firefighters serving NASA installations and Department of Defense facilities.

title: Told to Report for a Fitness-for-Duty Exam? Know Exactly What the Department Can and Can't Ask
excerpt: Fitness-for-duty referrals are becoming more common — and more legally fraught. Here's what the statutes and regulations actually require before an agency can send you for one, including the job-related, business-necessity standard that governs every such evaluation.

title: Coming Back From Leave and Getting Hit With a Fitness-for-Duty Order? Here's the Line the Law Draws
excerpt: Employers can require a fitness-for-duty evaluation after protected leave — but only within real limits. Courts are increasingly scrutinizing whether the referral is actually justified by a documented concern or functions instead as a pretext that discourages employees from using protected leave at all.

title: A City Told Firefighters Their Union Couldn't Talk Staffing With Elected Officials. The Union Sued.
excerpt: A First Amendment lawsuit over restrictions on union communication with elected officials is a reminder that meet-and-confer rights don't disappear the moment the conversation moves outside the bargaining room. Staffing levels and safety conditions are about as textbook a matter of public concern as it gets.

title: CAL FIRE Told Grieving Families There Was No State Death Benefit. Fourteen Families Say That Was a Lie.
excerpt: Families of contracted air tanker pilots killed fighting California wildfires allege CAL FIRE steered them toward a smaller federal benefit while sitting on a larger state entitlement it never disclosed. Fourteen families are seeking more than $4 million collectively over the alleged misrepresentation.

title: A $3.5 Million Verdict Just Got Wiped Out Because the Jury Was Handed the Wrong Rulebook
excerpt: The Court of Appeal reversed a wrongful death judgment against Buena Park police after finding the trial court applied a 2020 deadly force standard to a 2019 shooting — a timing error with a seven-figure price tag. The correct legal standard is always the one in effect on the date of the incident, not the one in effect by trial.

title: California Can't Punish You for Filing a 'False' Complaint Against an Officer Anymore — Here's Why That Cuts Both Ways
excerpt: The California Supreme Court strikes down the criminal penalty and warning requirement tied to filing a knowingly false complaint against a peace officer, finding the law unconstitutionally burdens protected speech.

title: POST Pulled 56 Badges Last Year Over Convictions Alone — Here's What Actually Triggers Decertification
excerpt: POST's 2025 annual report details a sharp rise in decertification actions tied to criminal convictions, with 56 revocations based on post-2022 felony or misdemeanor convictions and thousands of cases still in the pipeline.

title: Two Officers Were Indicted Over a Fatal Shooting Involving a Toy Gun. A Judge Just Ended the Case.
excerpt: A Los Angeles County judge dismisses the voluntary manslaughter case against two Torrance officers in the 2018 shooting death of Christopher Deandre Mitchell, at the request of prosecutors unable to meet their burden of proof.

title: Three Officers Were Charged With Manslaughter Over a Restraint Death. Here's What the Filing Actually Alleges.
excerpt: Alameda County's District Attorney charges three former Alameda police officers with involuntary manslaughter in the 2021 death of Mario Gonzalez, who died after being restrained face-down during a welfare check.

title: California May Soon Require Reasonable Suspicion Before Officers Can Even Ask for a Consent Search
excerpt: Senate Bill 277 would bar California officers from requesting consent to search a person or vehicle absent pre-existing reasonable suspicion of criminal activity, closing a long-used workaround to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement.

title: Your Department Can No Longer Keep Seized Property Without a Conviction — Here's the Current State of California Forfeiture Law
excerpt: California's 2016 civil asset forfeiture reform continues to shape how departments handle seized cash and property, requiring a criminal conviction before most forfeitures can proceed and closing the federal equitable-sharing workaround.

title: Threatening a School, Church, or Workplace Is Now Its Own Standalone Crime in California
excerpt: Senate Bill 19 creates a specific criminal offense for threats of mass violence against workplaces, schools, houses of worship, and medical facilities, giving officers a clearer charging path in cases that previously relied on general threat statutes.

title: Prop 36 Gave Officers New Felony Arrest Power for Theft and Drug Crimes. Two Years In, Here's What Changed.
excerpt: Two years after California voters approved Proposition 36, the measure has generated roughly 40,000 new felony arrests for drug and theft offenses, reshaping how officers can charge repeat offenders and organized retail theft.

title: California Just Made It Easier to Enforce Red Flag Orders — Here's What Changed for Officers in the Field
excerpt: Senate Bill 899 streamlines court enforcement of gun violence restraining orders, and a new Attorney General model policy gives departments updated guidance on when and how officers should pursue GVROs.

title: California Officers Can No Longer Wear Masks on Duty Without Identifying Themselves — What SB 627 Actually Requires
excerpt: Senate Bill 627, the "No Secret Police Act," prohibits California law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings while performing official duties and requires visible identification for plainclothes personnel, with a written public policy required from every agency.

title: A Union Can't Just Ask for Your Personnel File — PERB Confirms the Pitchess Process Still Applies
excerpt: PERB rules that unions seeking confidential peace officer personnel records must use the Pitchess process rather than a standard information request, even when the union is acting in its representational capacity.

title: A Discipline Case Went Through Termination, Reinstatement, and Termination Again — Here's How PERB Ruled
excerpt: PERB reverses an ALJ finding that the City of California City violated the MMBA when the City Manager, rather than the Police Chief, issued termination notices to three officers, finding the deviation from policy did not have a significant adverse effect once the officers had waived their Skelly rights.

title: A Fire Department and Its Union Filed Charges Against Each Other Over Job Specs. PERB Dismissed Both.
excerpt: PERB affirms dismissal of dueling unfair practice charges between the City of Compton and Compton Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2216, arising from parallel negotiations over job specifications and a successor MOU.

title: Two Firefighters Alleged Retaliation Against Orange County Fire Authority. PERB Dismissed Both Charges.
excerpt: PERB affirms dismissal of consolidated retaliation and interference charges brought by two Orange County Fire Authority firefighters, finding the amended charges still failed to state a prima facie case.

title: A Deputy Sued His Own Union for Failing to Represent Him. Here's Why PERB Dismissed the Case.
excerpt: PERB affirms dismissal of a duty-of-fair-representation charge filed by a deputy against the San Francisco Deputy Sheriffs' Association, reinforcing the high bar for proving a union breached its representational duty.

title: A CDCR Employee Alleged Bullying Over Extra Duties. Here's Why the Charge Didn't Survive PERB Review.
excerpt: PERB affirms dismissal of a Dills Act charge brought by a Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation employee alleging she was required to perform duties outside her classification and harassed when she objected.

title: A County Held New-Employee Orientations Without the Union in the Room. PERB Said That Violated the Law.
excerpt: PERB affirms that the County of San Mateo violated both the MMBA and the Public Employee Communication Chapter by holding new employee orientations without providing the union advance notice or access, ordering make-whole relief.

title: A City Changed the Rules on Incentive Pay and Then Demanded Money Back. PERB Ordered It Reversed.
excerpt: PERB affirms that the City of Pleasanton committed two separate unilateral changes when it altered its criteria for educational incentive pay and then sought reimbursement for past payments that no longer qualified under the new criteria.

title: A City Photographed Picketers Outside a Public Building. PERB Says That Alone Can Be an Unfair Practice.
excerpt: PERB reverses dismissal of a charge alleging the City of Novato interfered with protected picketing by photographing or creating the appearance of photographing employees engaged in a lawful demonstration.

title: Body-Worn Camera Policy Changes Are Bargainable — Here's the Legislative Push Making That Explicit
excerpt: Pending California legislation addressing body-worn camera policy would codify what PERB precedent has already suggested: changes to surveillance and recording policy touching employee discipline fall within the scope of representation.

title: LAFD's Union President Says the Mayor Retaliated Against Him for Criticizing Wildfire Staffing. He's Suing.
excerpt: Suspended United Firefighters of Los Angeles City president Freddy Escobar files a claim against Mayor Karen Bass alleging a campaign of retaliation after he publicly criticized LAFD staffing levels following the Palisades fire.

title: LAPD Learned the Hard Way That You Can't Implement New Terms Before Impasse Procedures Are Exhausted
excerpt: A foundational ERB precedent holds that unilateral implementation of bargaining proposals before exhausting the Employee Relations Ordinance's impasse procedures is a per se unfair practice — a rule that continues to shape how LAPD and city departments handle stalled negotiations.

title: LAPD Cancelled a Scheduled Arbitration Hearing Without the Union's Sign-Off. The Board Called That Unlawful.
excerpt: ERB precedent holds that a department's unilateral cancellation of a scheduled arbitration hearing, made over the union's objection and without the arbitrator's approval, constitutes an unlawful repudiation of the MOU's grievance and arbitration provisions.

title: LAFD Changed How It Fills Promotional Vacancies Without Bargaining First. Here's Why That Was Unlawful.
excerpt: ERB precedent establishes that procedures for filling vacancies in a newly created promotional class fall within the scope of bargaining because of their direct effect on terms and conditions of employment for LAFD personnel.

title: LAPD Barred Officers From Discussing an Ongoing Investigation With Each Other. The Board Upheld It.
excerpt: ERB precedent finds that a department's decision to prohibit employees from discussing events related to a pending personnel investigation is a legitimate business justification that defeats an interference claim, given the need to protect investigative integrity.

title: Serving as an Officer's Board of Rights Defense Rep Is Protected Conduct Under the ERO
excerpt: ERB precedent establishes that an officer's service as a defense representative in another officer's Board of Rights proceeding is protected conduct under the Employee Relations Ordinance, shielding the representative from retaliation tied to that role.

title: Full-Time Peace Officers Have a Statutory Right to Their Own Bargaining Unit — Here's the Case That Confirmed It
excerpt: ERB precedent confirms that full-time peace officers possess a statutory right to a bargaining unit exclusive to peace officers, supporting severance petitions to carve police-specific units out of broader, mixed-classification bargaining units.

title: LAFD Removed Firefighters From the Risk Management Program. The City Still Had to Bargain the Effects.
excerpt: ERB precedent holds that even when a management decision is fundamental enough to fall outside the scope of bargaining, its effects on employees — such as removal from a risk management or benefits program — must still be negotiated.

title: How Long Does a Workplace Practice Have to Exist Before the City Can't Change It Without Bargaining?
excerpt: ERB precedent explains the standard for when an unwritten workplace practice becomes a protected condition of employment that a department cannot alter unilaterally, requiring the practice to exist long enough to become a legitimate employee expectation.

title: LA City and County Just Got the Same Strike Protections Every Other California Public Employer's Unions Already Had
excerpt: Assembly Bill 2889 fixes a drafting gap that had left the City of Los Angeles Employee Relations Board and the LA County Employee Relations Commission outside a decade-old statutory protection against strike-preparation damages, and gives PERB exclusive initial jurisdiction over related injunctive relief.

title: LA County Ordered Deputies to Answer Questions About Gang Tattoos. A Court Said the County Had to Bargain First.
excerpt: The California Court of Appeal affirms an injunction requiring Los Angeles County to complete effects bargaining with ALADS before compelling deputies to sit for interviews and photograph tattoos as part of a law enforcement gang investigation.

title: LA County Admitted It Violated the Law When It Subpoenaed Deputies' Personnel Files Without Bargaining
excerpt: Los Angeles County settles unfair practice charges brought by ALADS and PPOA, admitting it violated the Employee Relations Ordinance when the Civilian Oversight Commission subpoenaed confidential personnel records without first negotiating the effects with either union.

title: ERCOM's 2022 Ruling on Oversight Subpoena Power Is Still Shaping County Labor Disputes Today
excerpt: An ERCOM decision finds Los Angeles County violated the Employee Relations Ordinance by implementing an ordinance expanding Civilian Oversight Commission subpoena power without first negotiating its effects with ALADS, a ruling still cited in subsequent disputes.

title: What ERCOM Actually Does — And Why It Doesn't Hear Your Discipline Appeal
excerpt: A breakdown of the Los Angeles County Employee Relations Commission's structure and jurisdiction, including what kinds of disputes it resolves and the specific category of cases — discipline matters — that fall outside its authority entirely.

title: LA County's Public Defenders Union Has Filed Multiple Unfair Practice Charges — Here's the Pattern
excerpt: The LA County Public Defenders Union has brought successive unfair practice charges against the County Public Defender's Office, reflecting recurring tension over working conditions and bargaining obligations within a county department under chronic resource strain.

title: SEIU Filed an Unfair Practice Charge Against the County's Chief Executive Office. Here's What ERCOM Decided.
excerpt: ERCOM issues a Decision and Order in an unfair practice dispute between Service Employees International Union Local 721 and the Los Angeles County Chief Executive Office, underscoring the commission's ongoing role adjudicating labor disputes across county departments.

title: An AFSCME Local Took the County's Children's Services Department to ERCOM. The Case Shows How the Process Works.
excerpt: A 2019 unfair practice decision involving AFSCME Local 1083 and the County's Community and Senior Services Department illustrates the standard procedural path ERCOM cases follow from charge to final commission order.

title: How LA County Firefighters' Bargaining Units Actually Get Structured — And Why It Matters
excerpt: A look at how ERCOM handles bargaining unit accretion and structure requests for Los Angeles County Fire Department classifications represented by IAFF Local 1014, and why unit configuration decisions carry long-term consequences for negotiating leverage.

title: Negotiations With LA County Stalled? Here's What Fact-Finding and Mediation Actually Look Like at ERCOM
excerpt: A breakdown of ERCOM's impasse resolution tools — mediation and fact-finding — and how Los Angeles County bargaining units, including Sheriff's Department and Fire Department units, can use these processes when direct negotiations with the County stall.

title: Which Unions Actually Represent LA County Employees? ERCOM's Certified List Answers That.
excerpt: ERCOM maintains the official list of certified employee organizations authorized to represent Los Angeles County bargaining units, including ALADS and PPOA for sworn law enforcement personnel, and the list is a critical reference point in any representation dispute.

title: Fired First, Disabled Second? The CalPERS Case That Says the Order Matters
excerpt: Haywood v. American River Fire Protection District holds that a firefighter terminated for cause before applying for disability retirement can be barred from receiving it — making timing one of the most consequential decisions in any discipline-adjacent disability claim.

title: CalPERS Quietly Raised the Bar for Approving Your Disability Retirement
excerpt: CalPERS now requires contracting agencies to submit substantially more documentation before certifying a local safety member's disability retirement application, a shift that has slowed approvals and increased denials for police and fire applicants statewide.

title: Who Actually Controls Your Retirement Board? The Supreme Court Just Answered
excerpt: The California Supreme Court rules that county retirement boards operating under CERL do not have final authority over job classifications and salaries for their own staff — that power stays with the county board of supervisors.

title: LACERA Made You Wait Years for Your Disability Pension — Turns Out It Doesn't Owe You Interest
excerpt: Weber v. Board of Retirement holds that LACERA has no statutory authority to pay interest on the retroactive lump sum owed to members whose disability retirement applications take years to process.

title: He Had a Heart Attack Skiing in Colorado — Why His Firefighter Pension Claim Still Failed
excerpt: Geoghegan v. Retirement Board shows how the heart-trouble presumption for firefighters and police can be rebutted with evidence the real cause was something entirely outside the job.

title: Your Department Can't Interrogate You Without This Warning — The Case That Made It Law
excerpt: Lybarger v. City of Los Angeles establishes that officers ordered to answer questions in an internal affairs interrogation must be told their statements can't be used against them criminally, or the department loses the right to use silence against them.

title: The County Didn't Have to Be Cruel — Just Wrong. That Was Enough to Lose.
excerpt: Wallace v. County of Stanislaus holds that a good-faith, honest mistake about a deputy's fitness for duty is still disability discrimination if it results in an adverse employment action — no ill will required.

title: The California Supreme Court Just Decided How Much of Your Pension Promise Is Actually Safe
excerpt: Alameda County Deputy Sheriffs' Assn. v. Alameda County Employees' Retirement Assn. upholds PEPRA's narrowing of 'compensation earnable,' leaving the California Rule on vested pension rights intact but showing its real limits.

title: Win the Federal Case, and the State Wrongful Death Suit Can Die With It
excerpt: Hernandez v. City of Pomona holds that a federal judgment finding an officer's use of deadly force objectively reasonable can collaterally estop a follow-on state wrongful death claim built around the same shooting, even when plaintiffs try to reframe it around pre-shooting tactics.

title: CalPERS Tried to Deny Her Pension Over a Job That Existed Only in Theory
excerpt: McCormick v. CalPERS holds that a disability retirement applicant is eligible when she can no longer perform her duties at the only location her employer will allow her to work, even if she could theoretically work elsewhere, and that requesting an accommodation is not a prerequisite to eligibility.
